# University of Sydney Summary
The University of Sydney, founded in 1850, is Australia’s oldest university and one of the first public, non-denominational, and secular universities in the British Empire. It pioneered merit-based admission and was among the earliest to admit women equally (from 1881). Its main campus in Camperdown/Darlington is renowned for Neo-Gothic architecture and is home to leading faculties such as Arts and Social Sciences, Medicine and Health, Business, Science, and Engineering. The university has expanded to include specialist campuses, research stations, and key affiliate colleges, as well as the state-of-the-art Chau Chak Wing Museum. The University Library is the largest academic library in the Southern Hemisphere and is the only Australian university with state legal deposit library status.
Globally recognized, Sydney ranks #25 (QS, 2026), #53 (THE, 2026), and #29 (US News, 2025–26), consistently placing in the top three nationally. Its graduates are highly employable, with strong employer satisfaction and early-career salary outcomes. Alumni include eight Australian prime ministers, several Nobel laureates, and prominent figures in law, science, arts, and international affairs. The university offers extensive student life programmes, scholarships, affiliated and owned accommodation, and is home to the country's oldest and largest university student union. Recent decades have seen significant growth, modernization initiatives, and controversies, including issues related to student satisfaction, sexual misconduct, and staff underpayment.
